INFLATION_DEF.label: Definition of inflation (sustained rise in general price level)

stages.name: Inflation: causes and effects
stages.title: Inflation: causes and effects
stages.sub: Explain what pushes prices up economy-wide, and trace the effects on consumers, firms and trade.

steps.q: Economists draw total spending in the economy against total output, to see what drives the general price level. What kind of tool is this: a picture of one shop's price, or a picture of the whole economy?
steps.right: A picture of the whole economy
steps.wrong: A picture of one shop's price
steps.hint: Inflation is a rise in the general price level, across everything, not just one good.

steps.q: Consumers get a wave of confidence and spend much more, but factories cannot suddenly produce much more. If total spending races ahead of what the economy can supply, what happens to the general price level?
steps.hint: More money chasing a roughly fixed amount of output has to show up somewhere.

steps.q: Oil and wages both become far more expensive, so it costs firms much more to produce the same output at every price. If firms need higher prices just to cover these higher costs, what happens to the general price level?
steps.hint: Firms will only supply the same amount if they can charge more to cover their higher costs.

steps.q: Your wage stays at £2,000 a month but, because of demand-pull or cost-push pressure, prices across the shops rise by 10%. Can you buy as much as before with that same £2,000?
steps.wrong: Yes, exactly the same as before
steps.hint: The number on your payslip has not changed, but what that money buys has.

steps.q: A supermarket now has to reprint every price label, and it cannot tell if next month's costs will jump again when planning a new store. Is running the business now easier or harder than when prices were stable?
steps.right: Harder, with extra costs and uncertainty
steps.wrong: Easier, since prices just rise anyway
steps.hint: Think about the cost of changing every price tag, and the difficulty of planning ahead.

steps.q: Rising costs push a UK firm's prices up faster than a French rival's prices, while both sell the same product abroad. Which one will foreign buyers now prefer?
steps.right: The French rival, now relatively cheaper
steps.wrong: The UK firm, since it costs more to make
steps.hint: Foreign buyers compare prices between countries, not just look at cost of production.
